title: Tumefactive demyelinating disease with isolated spinal cord involvement
case_prompt:
A 31-year-old woman with no significant past medical history presented with acute onset of lumbar pain, bladder incontinence, and gait imbalance. Over several days, her symptoms progressed to paraplegia with complete loss of motor and sensory function below the T4 level. 

Initial MRI of the spine showed abnormal T2 hyperintensity extending from C6 through the upper thoracic cord, with mild cord expansion and faint enhancement in the lower thoracic region. She was treated with high-dose corticosteroids, intravenous immunoglobulin, and underwent rehabilitation. Two months later, her clinical status remained unchanged, but repeat MRI demonstrated significant improvement of the cervical and thoracic cord signal abnormalities, with only small residual foci.

Six months after the initial presentation, she experienced acute upper thoracic pain and dysesthesias radiating to the ulnar aspect of both upper extremities. MRI of the spine revealed marked interval worsening of signal abnormalities with avid enhancement at T6 to T8 and a focal exophytic component at T7. MRI of the brain was normal. A spinal angiogram showed no vascular malformation or dural fistula. CT scans of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis revealed no evidence of lymphoma. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis demonstrated elevated protein and lymphocytic pleocytosis, with no malignant cells and negative neuromyelitis optica IgG. Autoimmune and infectious serologies, including tests for Sjögren’s syndrome, systemic lupus erythematosus, Lyme disease, HIV, HTLV, and hepatitis, were unremarkable.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Primary CNS tumor or lymphoma considered — “CNS lymphoma can improve following steroid therapy; however, CSF serology, and chest, abdomen, and pelvic computed tomography (CT) imaging for the presence of lymphoma were negative.”  
2. Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder considered — “no neuromyeltis optica (NMO) IgG or neoplastic cytology.”  
3. Other idiopathic inflammatory demyelinating disorders considered — “Other IIDDs associated with tumefactive demyelination are NMO, acute disseminated encephalomyelitis, acute hemorrhagic leukoencephalomyelitis, Balo concentric sclerosis, Marburg acute MS, and Schilder’s disease…are easily ruled out based on disease involvement and progression.”  
4. Infectious etiologies considered — “Autoimmune and infectious serologies including Sjogren, Lupus, Lyme, HIV, HTLV, and hepatitis were all unremarkable.”  
5. Tumefactive demyelination (MS variant) favored by relapsing–remitting course and steroid responsiveness — “three observations are key to the diagnosis of TMS: (i) the presence of intracranial periventricular lesions; (ii) a relapsing-remitting course rather than a slow progressive trend; and (iii) response to steroid therapy on follow-up imaging.”
